sm: The host opens by describing an ABC World News Tonight segment about two University of Mississippi students who made chest-beating and monkey-like noises outside a Black student's apartment, caught on a doorbell camera. He argues the story should never have been national news, says Ole Miss prejudged the investigation, and says it is not clear the women knew who lived there. He claims that stories of white people making monkey noises as a racist gesture are almost always fake or irrelevant, and he uses a bus analogy to suggest that the people calling the noises racist are the ones making the association.

The host plays a Good Morning America report saying the video had been viewed more than eleven million times, and notes that it mentioned a similar 2024 incident at Ole Miss. He argues that the 2024 frat student was engaged in protected speech under the First Amendment. He then cites a TMZ report in which an eighteen-year-old freshman said she had never met the women and did not know their race, and that the girls made animal noises at several doors. He says that if true, the women should sue the media, the school and the activists who published their information. He compares the case to Covington Catholic and contrasts it with the left's defense of comedian Dave Chappelle.

The host says one of the women apologized and withdrew from the university because of threats, and he compares that with how he says other cases were handled. He plays a clip of a Black student saying she felt unsafe, and he mocks the idea that a slur at a doorbell camera would be frightening. He claims such an incident would instead benefit the person, and says Black liberals have no theory of mind for white people. He also says the police-shooting narrative is similarly overblown and that claims of racism by white cops are not supported by body camera evidence.

The host argues that even hearing a slur is not a reason to feel unsafe, because words protected by the First Amendment should rank low among life's grievances. He says Ole Miss cannot punish protected speech and that this should not be a national story. He then plays a CBS News segment with the Black women who live in the apartment, including Jekaira Metcalf and Victoria Johnson. He mocks its dramatic language, its mention that Ole Miss admitted its first Black student in 1962, and the students describing themselves as devastated. He notes that the girls told them they had made the noises at other doors, and that one of them apologized.

The host plays the Black students saying they do not fully forgive the apology and that the women should be accountable, and he says apologizing to such people is pointless. He says the student, named as Alina Kunez, withdrew from the university after harassment. He contrasts the coverage with a York College incident in which he says a white woman was dragged off her porch and beaten, and with the shooting of fifteen-year-old Austin Payne in Albany, Georgia. He reads the names of the five suspects, and lists major outlets he says have not covered it. He calls the Ole Miss story a revival of 2020-style cancellation and says it now reaches the student's family.

A local news clip says Kunez is the granddaughter of the owner of Kunez Auto Group in Wisconsin. The host then discusses a TMZ report on a lawsuit by a Black woman against the family's Buick GMC dealership, saying an employee printed a racial slur on a sticker that went onto her windshield. He says the employee was fired and argues it was likely a mistake, and he calls this collective punishment. He then turns to a Montgomery County, Maryland event condemning a lynching from 1896, and he says no lynching has happened in the country this century. He notes that the man lynched, Sidney Randolph, had been accused of killing a seven-year-old girl with an axe.

The host lists the evidence against Randolph, including a woodcutter who saw him with an axe, matching footprints, and a jacket, and says it is not possible to re-litigate the 1896 case. He argues that without forensic tools, communities had to choose between letting murderers go free and using extrajudicial methods. He says activists ignore this and want money from the government over old trauma. He then plays a CNN panel exchange in which a woman says Black fathers are present at a higher rate than other fathers. He rejects this and says Black fatherlessness is about seventy percent, or fifty percent by a more generous measure, and says she is relying on personal anecdote against data.

The host says the midterms and the rise of the left will make things dumber and that anti-white grievance and wokeness are back. He mocks a video of a senator-elect being credited with lowering gas prices before taking office. He says Trump's two victories did not end the race hoaxes, citing Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown, George Floyd and Jacob Blake as earlier examples. He warns that the TikTok mob will target families and businesses and describes this as Woke 2.0. He advises parents to tell their children heading to college or work to recognize the threat. He ends with a goodbye and a plug for the Daily Wire film Confession, premiering that night at seven Eastern.
